The report doesn't contain any numerical lab values in the traditional sense (e.g., blood tests, etc). Instead, it presents macroscopic and microscopic findings from the skin biopsies. The macroscopic examination details the size and appearance of the tissue samples. The microscopic examination of the right thigh biopsy shows mild orthokeratosis (thickening of the outer skin layer), thinned epidermis (the outer layer of skin), intraepidermal and suprabasal blistering (fluid-filled sacs within the epidermis), spongiosis (fluid accumulation in the epidermis), basal vacuolar degeneration (damage to the basal layer of the epidermis), and dense acute and chronic inflammation in the dermis (the deeper layer of skin). Leucocytoclastic vasculitis (inflammation and damage to small blood vessels) is also noted. The left thigh biopsy shows similar features, including bullae (blisters) in the intraepidermal and subrabasal regions with necrosis (cell death) and neutrophilic debris (dead white blood cells). Basal vacuolar degeneration is also present. The left thigh shows dense infiltration of various inflammatory cells, including neutrophils, eosinophils, histiocytes, and lymphocytes. The report concludes that the features are suggestive of Behçet's disease. This is a rare inflammatory disorder that affects blood vessels throughout the body, most noticeably the skin, mucous membranes, eyes, and nervous system. Absence of subcutaneous tissue prevented an assessment of panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat). The absence of quantitative lab values means there's no numerical data to assess against normal ranges.
